paras: The expulsion of R. Baxter McRary was the forced departure of a wealthy Black real estate dealer and Masonic grand master from Lexington, North Carolina, in August 1920, after white citizens found him hiding beneath the home of editor H. B. Varner. After a night in jail he was told through the mayor to leave town or risk his safety, and he left. Varner then sued him for $100,000, and Black papers asked why McRary had not been lynched and whether the affair was a scheme to take his wealth.

North Carolina papers called McRary "a mulatto with large holdings" and long the grand master of the state's Black Masons; the Baltimore Afro-American added that he was 55, a Lincoln University graduate and a former justice of the peace. Varner owned the Lexington Dispatch and chaired the state prison board.

According to a Lexington dispatch, citizens told that McRary had entered Varner's home "by stealth" during earlier absences set a watch on a Monday night while Varner was in New York. The Afro-American's report was dated August 14, which places that Monday on August 9. The watchers saw McRary enter about 10 o'clock, placed guards around the lot and searched the house in vain.

Between 12:30 and 1 o'clock Tuesday morning a spotlight found him under the floor, where he had crawled from the basement. He spent the rest of the night in jail, which the Monroe Journal said he "gladly" accepted; the Afro-American said the crowd "landed him in the city hall." That morning prominent citizens sent Mayor J. T. Hedrick to tell him to leave without delay and that any return would be "at his peril." The Elizabeth City Independent said he obeyed "with alacrity," and his whereabouts were unknown.

Varner returned, sued in Davidson County superior court, attached McRary's holdings and sued his wife for divorce; Mrs. Varner went to Kentucky. On September 25 a Lexington report said no answer had been filed, and Varner's attorneys said any judgment would go to charity and that McRary "had fled." No report of a criminal charge against McRary, of action against the men who seized him, or of the suit's outcome appears in the coverage.

North Carolina's white papers treated the expulsion as a prelude to the lawsuit; the Monroe Journal called McRary "the miscreant," and both it and the Independent said he had "posed as a moral uplifter" of his race. The Abbeville Press and Banner headlined the story "Negro Run Out Of Town," while the Hickory Daily Record called it "a terrible affair" but wondered why Varner wanted money damages. Elsewhere an Associated Press dispatch reported only the suit, and a fuller Raleigh dispatch carried the search to papers as far as South Dakota.

Black papers reprinted the Raleigh story, credited to the Chicago Tribune, and added their own comment. Under "Our People Protest!" the Cleveland Gazette asked, "Why was not McRary lynched? Is it a conspiracy to get the man's money?" The Chicago Broad Ax's editor suggested the scheme was "hatched up" to take his property, and in the New York Age James Weldon Johnson asked why the citizens had not raised "the cry of rape" and lynched him. The Chicago Whip condemned "the mayor and citizens of Raleigh" who forced him out, the Black Dispatch quoted his brethren calling it "the badger game," and the Afro-American later reported a belief that he was being blackmailed. Where white papers told a scandal about a Black man and a white woman, Black papers focused on the expulsion and the absence of a lynching.

Some Black papers placed events in Raleigh, a wire dateline, while the North Carolina accounts place them in Lexington. The Chicago Whip said he was found "in Mrs. Varner's apartment" rather than under the floor, and the Chicago Defender said he refused to leave until the suit followed. A Philadelphia Tribune dispatch claimed that Varner owed McRary about $24,000 and was not in New York but waiting for his watchers' signal; Varner's bankers said his only debt had been paid.

reader.title: Expulsion of R. Baxter McRary from Lexington, North Carolina
bases: Lexington citizens seized McRary at night, held him in jail, and through the mayor ordered him to leave town under threat to his safety; no assault is reported (A6, A11, A12).
The Lexington dispatch (A6), the separate Raleigh wire story (A7) and the Afro-American's Lexington correspondent (A11) agree on the night watch, capture, jailing and order to leave.

accounts.label: Lexington dispatch (North Carolina papers)
accounts.gist: Citizens set a watch, found McRary under the floor by spotlight between 12:30 and 1 a.m., jailed him, and a citizens' conference sent the mayor to warn him to leave or face peril; he left.

accounts.label: Raleigh wire story (Chicago Tribune)
accounts.gist: Citizens surrounded the house, threw flashlights on the cellar and caught him under the floor; he was arrested and warned by Mayor Hedrick to flee.

accounts.label: Afro-American Lexington correspondent
accounts.gist: The crowd located him and 'landed him in the city hall'; on the mayor's advice he was told to leave town and return at his peril.

accounts.label: Chicago Defender
accounts.gist: Varner's friends took him from the home to the mayor's office, where he was told to leave; he refused and the suit followed.

accounts.label: Chicago Whip
accounts.gist: He was found in Mrs. Varner's apartment and taken in charge by the mayor, who made his escape from the state possible; locals called the release a ruse to rob him.

accounts.label: Philadelphia Tribune via Afro-American
accounts.gist: McRary was a frequent guest and creditor of Varner, who was not in New York but waiting for his watchers' signal; the trap was deliberate.

accounts.label: Varner's attorneys and bankers
accounts.gist: Any judgment would go to charity, McRary had fled and was contemplating disposing of his property, and Varner's only debt had been paid.

framing.detail: Monroe Journal: 'VARNER SUES A NEGRO', McRary 'the miscreant', a 'wealthy mulatto' who 'posed as a moral uplifter'; the expulsion is told without criticism.
Elizabeth City Independent: he 'posed as a moral uplifter' and obeyed the order to leave 'with alacrity'.
Hickory Daily Record: 'a terrible affair'; McRary 'disappeared at the instance of Lexington men', but questions why Varner wants money damages.
AP Durham dispatch on the suit only, headlined 'SUES NEGRO FOR $100,000 FOR WRECKING HIS HOME'.
Raleigh dispatch 'WHITE EDITOR SUES NEGRO', 'Southern Society Shocked'; search and mayor's warning reported as fact.
Cleveland Gazette 'OUR PEOPLE PROTEST!': 'Why was not McRary lynched? Is it a conspiracy to get the man's money?'
Chicago Broad Ax editor: the scheme may have been hatched to grab McRary's property.
Chicago Whip: release with orders to flee was 'southern treachy'; 'Under the Lash' condemns the mayor and citizens who forced him out.
New York Age (James Weldon Johnson): asks why no lynching and gives 'an entirely new economic slant on the question of lynching', while calling Varner's suit the 'only civilized' step.
Omaha Monitor: 'Believed Conspiracy to Mulet Him'; Black Dispatch: 'the badger game on a big scale'; Afro-American: blackmail rumor and 'Exiled'.
Baltimore Afro-American first report 'Scandal Stirs Carolina Town' gives biography and the search without comment.
